doc.title: Billy Taylor interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995

title: Segregation made great musicians accessible
summary: Taylor says racial separation pressed Ellington and Basie into the black community, so young musicians could reach them.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Let me ask you something about that. Okay, sometimes, and this is just my opinion, I feel that as far as the music goes, as far as jazz goes, that the racial separation actually did blacks some good. Because it made ‘em play together.

Not only did it make us play together, what happened is that the Duke Ellingtons, the Count Basies and the every strata of the music was available because they had nowhere else to go. We were all pressed into the black community. So everyone was accessible. I mean a man of Duke Ellington’s stature, a man of Count Basie’s stature, today would live, perhaps, in an area that I as a young musician couldn’t afford. So therefore he would not be as accessible as if he lived upstairs in the apartment above me you know, as many of them did.
